## TL;DR

This follow-up closes the remaining failure-reporting and provider-parity gaps for remote validation and browser captures. Docker/SSH failures in startup cleanup are now logged without aborting prerequisite probing, while a failed watchdog or cancellation removal remains a real failure that preserves run state and its host slot. The non-Tailscale runner also has cancellation behavior matching the Tailscale path. Round-one review found that stale-container cleanup was the one exception to its documented best-effort contract; that behavior is now corrected and covered by executable regression tests.

## Work and rationale

The central decision was to preserve two different contracts for Docker removal. Startup prerequisite probing performs opportunistic cleanup of stale containers. It is not a run or a health check of the Docker daemon itself, and its caller chains commands with `&&`; therefore, an unavailable Docker list or an unsuccessful removal must not make an otherwise reachable host fail its probe. The startup cleanup now reports list and removal errors to stderr but returns success, allowing the rest of the probe to proceed. It keeps the name-prefix and stopped-state filters, and verifies the inspected name before removing anything. The watchdog and explicit cancellation paths have the opposite contract: they must not release the slot or settle the run while a container may still exist. Those paths continue to propagate removal failure, with Docker's “No such container” response treated as already removed.

The startup reaper in `validate.sh` was swept as a whole. Docker listing, inspection, logs, stats, and removal are guarded individually, emit diagnostics on failure, and let the validation run continue. This avoids letting one transient inspection or diagnostic command abort unrelated validation work while ensuring failures are visible.

Cancellation handling was aligned across runner providers. A capture cancellation attempts to remove the specific run's container, records failure when remote removal cannot be confirmed, and preserves the active run and slot until cleanup is known to have completed. This keeps the event stream and logs honest instead of claiming successful removal after an SSH or Docker error.

The round-one review identified a narrower issue in `staleContainerCleanupCommand()`: its list and removal failures propagated through the prerequisite probe even though the call-site comment explicitly required best-effort cleanup. I kept the change local to this startup-only consumer and added execution-level tests with a fake Docker CLI. The tests force `docker ps` and `docker rm` to fail, assert the emitted diagnostics, and require the cleanup command to exit successfully. This leaves the stricter kill command semantics untouched.

## Approaches tried

I first preserved the failure exit from stale cleanup, following the removal-failure handling used by watchdog and cancel operations. Review correctly pointed out that the startup probe has a distinct best-effort contract: failing there turns an incidental cleanup problem into host unavailability. I changed only the stale cleanup command to log and continue, and retained precise failure propagation for active-run removal.

The initial regression test run exposed a shell-output capture mistake: redirecting only the final command did not capture a diagnostic emitted outside the pipeline. Grouping the generated command before redirecting fixed the test harness, and both forced-failure cases then passed.

## Challenges and blockers

The first full scoped check found formatter differences in the two edited files after passing its remote build, tests, and browser checks. I ran the repository formatter and repeated the complete check. That attempt had one failure in an unrelated real-process test for the managed-agent `repoos serve` guard on Bee. The same test passed when run locally in isolation, so I reran the full check rather than modifying unrelated serving behavior. The final full check passed remotely on Bee and completed all local guards successfully.

The final validation ran build and 154 changed-path test files: 2,744 passed and one was skipped. Rendered contrast, UI smoke, formatting, lint, and other selected local checks passed. RepoOS created WIP checkpoint commits for the checked source tree; I did not stage or commit manually.

## Key learnings

Best-effort cleanup is only best-effort if its command exits successfully all the way through its shell composition. A helper's failure semantics must be chosen for its caller: swallowing a removal error is wrong when the caller owns an active run, but propagating it from unrelated startup cleanup can incorrectly mark a healthy host unreachable. Executable command tests helped verify the actual shell exit behavior and diagnostics, beyond checking the generated command text.
